 Christmas Eve to Become a Public Holiday in Hungary This Year
 Hungary Today 
 2026.11.04. 
 Print without picture 
 Print with picture 
 The Parliament has declared December 24 a public holiday, effective immediately this year, giving workers a four-day Christmas weekend. In a rare show of unanimity, the National Assembly passed the amendment with 193 votes in favor and none against or abstaining. 
 The change brings the total number of consecutive public holidays at Christmas to three. The new legislation has immediate implications for the entire December work calendar. Under the previously established working-time schedule for 2026, December 24, a Thursday, had been designated as a regular day off that employees would have had to make up by working an additional Saturday shift on December 12.
 Now that Christmas Eve has become a separate statutory public holiday, there is no longer a reason for that schedule adjustment.
 December 12 will once again be a regular Saturday off for employees working under the standard working-time arrangement.
 The formal amendment to the relevant ministerial implementing regulation is expected shortly.
 For businesses, the decision means much more than simply changing a date on the wall calendar. Consulting firm Niveus cautions employers against treating the change as a purely technical adjustment. Human resources and payroll departments will face a series of additional labor-law and administrative obligations:
 Reviewing existing work schedules and vacation plans: All shift schedules for December 12 and 24 must be revised. Vacation time already approved for December 12 must be reclassified or credited back in accordance with the ministerial regulation, since employees will no longer be required to work that day.
 Recalculating working-time arrangements: For businesses operating under flexible working-time schedules or longer accounting periods, the required working hours will decrease. These adjustments must be formally documented and communicated to employees in writing.
 Shift work and irregular working hours: Where working hours differ from the standard arrangement, employers must separately determine how both dates are classified under the Hungarian Labor Code.
 “Year-end scheduling cannot be reduced to a simple technical calendar adjustment. All changes must be implemented thoroughly and consistently from both a labor-law and payroll perspective,” said Szandra Bartók, Payroll Manager at Niveus.
 Under Hungarian law, public holidays enjoy greater legal protection than ordinary days off.
 Going forward, employers may require employees to work on December 24 only under narrowly defined statutory exceptions. These include businesses operating continuous shifts, seasonal operations, essential public services, and cross-border services.
 If employees are legally required to work on Christmas Eve, they are entitled to the statutory public holiday premium of 100%. Adjustments are also necessary for employees paid by the hour or based on performance who remain at home that day. Under certain statutory conditions, they are entitled to compensation for the hours they would otherwise have worked. This payment will generally be equivalent to eight hours of regular pay.
 While employees can look forward to a welcome break and uninterrupted holiday celebrations without having to make up the day beforehand, company executives and payroll departments have little time to spare before mid-December. Everything from time-tracking systems and attendance records to interim tax and payroll contribution calculations must be promptly updated to reflect the new legal requirements.
